title: Between the Facts and the Promise. Hope Without Illusions.
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Callahan, Steven, Adrift: Seventy-Six Days Lost at Sea, Houghton Mifflin 1986
Galef, Julia, The Scout Mindset: Why Some People See Things Clearly and Others Don’t, Portfolio 2021, ch. 7
Maier, Steven F.; Seligman, Martin E. P., Learned Helplessness at Fifty: Insights from Neuroscience, “Psychological Review” 123 (2016)
Malouff, John M.; Schutte, Nicola S., Can Psychological Interventions Increase Optimism? A Meta-Analysis, “The Journal of Positive Psychology” 12 (2017)
Robertson, Dougal, Sea Survival: A Manual, Praeger 1975
Seligman, Martin E. P., Learned Optimism, Knopf 1991
Seligman, Martin E. P.; Schulman, Peter, Explanatory Style as a Predictor of Productivity and Quitting Among Life Insurance Sales Agents, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 50 (1986)
Snyder, Charles R., The Psychology of Hope: You Can Get There from Here, Free Press 1994
Snyder, C. R.; Shorey, Hal S.; Cheavens, Jennifer; Pulvers, Kimberley M.; Adams, Virgil H.; Wiklund, Cynthia, Hope and Academic Success in College, “Journal of Educational Psychology” 94 (2002)

paragraphs: After a failure, each of us tells ourselves a short story in our head. The pessimistic version goes something like this: “It will always be like this, everything falls apart for me, because that’s just the way I am.” The optimistic version says that the trouble will pass and concerns only this one matter, and that my mistake was just one of many possible causes of the failure. The psychologist Martin Seligman called this mechanism explanatory style and examined what effect it has on everyday life. The insurance agents he studied who had a more optimistic explanatory style sold noticeably more policies and were less likely to quit their jobs. Importantly, this kind of optimism can be learned: when you catch yourself thinking “I’ll never manage it,” check whether that claim is really based on the facts.

Yet this valuable skill has its limits. Optimism remains a forecast about my chances, and an honest forecast has to take the facts into account. In the face of a serious diagnosis, or after the death of someone close, positive thinking alone is no longer enough.

In his Letter to the Romans, the apostle Paul describes a man who, humanly speaking, had no grounds left for optimism. Abraham was about a hundred years old, and his wife Sarah had long been unable to have children. Yet God promised him descendants as numerous as the stars. Paul stresses that Abraham took a hard look at his worn-out body and did not pretend to be younger, and yet his faith did not waver. “Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed” (Romans 4:18), because he was convinced that God had the power to do what He had promised.

This is exactly where the line runs between optimism and biblical hope. Optimism rests on an assessment of my chances, while biblical hope rests on the character of the One who made the promise. The Letter to the Hebrews compares this hope to an anchor, firm and secure, that reaches into a reality invisible from the deck. Jesus entered there first, opening the way for us too.

The New Testament says plainly what this certainty rests on. Christian hope grows out of the resurrection of Jesus and His promise that He will return, and that then those who died trusting Him will rise. God does not promise that everything will turn out the way we want. What He does promise is His presence, His faithfulness, and the morning of the resurrection. Whoever has an anchor like that can look calmly at the facts and has no need to dress them up. They do what they can and leave the rest to God, whose faithfulness does not depend on human odds.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: What do I rest my hope on when the facts are no longer on my side?
challenge: Before you put your phone down today or close your computer, recall one failure from the past few days and think about the story you tell yourself about it. Does the word “always” or “never” appear in that story? Consider on Whom, or on what, you want to rest your hope today.

paragraphs: In February 1982, about a week after setting sail from the Canary Islands, Steven Callahan’s small yacht took on water during a night storm and sank. The sailor managed to jump into an inflatable life raft and pull some equipment out of the sinking boat. The Caribbean islands, toward which the current and the wind were carrying him, lay about three thousand kilometers away, and the drift would last eleven weeks.

It is easy to think that Callahan survived because he was an incurable optimist, but the book he wrote after his return shows something quite different. The castaway counted his water down to the last sip and worked out that he could allow himself one sip roughly every six hours. He kept navigation notes and, with every week, honestly widened the margin of error in his estimate of where he actually was. Whenever a ship appeared on the horizon, he coolly calculated whether it was worth firing one of his few flares, and even so, several vessels passed him by without noticing the raft. He speared the fish circling beneath the raft and collected water from rain and from small solar stills. He also frankly noted what had worked in his favor: before the voyage he had swapped his raft for a larger one. On a smaller one it would have been hard to hold out for so many weeks.

In the worst moments he told himself that he was doing everything he could, and that nothing more depended on him. He allowed himself to think about imminent rescue only very cautiously. From the sinking yacht he had taken a manual written by another castaway, and he remembered its advice to treat rescue as a welcome interruption of one’s own fight for survival. On the seventy-sixth day, fishermen from a small island near Guadeloupe noticed birds circling over the raft. By then Callahan had lost more than a third of his body weight, and yet he still had more than two liters of water in his containers.
What kept him alive, when the weather was against him and the chances of a quick rescue were slim? Is it a gift that some people have and others don’t, or a skill that can be learned?

sections.heading: What Do You Tell Yourself When You Lose?
paragraphs: Psychology offers a partial answer to that question. In the 1960s, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, psychologists at the University of Pennsylvania, studied the behavior of dogs exposed to inescapable electric shocks. Animals that had learned they had no control over ending the unpleasant stimuli often did not try to escape even when they were later given a real chance to avoid the shocks. This was the birth of the concept of learned helplessness. Seligman began to wonder: if helplessness can be learned, can its opposite be learned too? That question became one of the starting points for the concept of learned optimism, which he later developed in a book of that very title.

Half a century later, together with Steven Maier, he took stock of the research on learned helplessness. In a 2016 article, the two scientists argued that the original explanation of its mechanism had been the wrong way around. Passivity is not a learned response but the organism’s default response to prolonged threatening stimuli. What the brain learns is something else: that we can influence what happens. So we might say that our hope is built by small pieces of evidence that we can still do something. That is exactly the kind of evidence Callahan gave himself every day, with every fish he caught and every sip of water he saved.

Seligman and his colleagues also described a phenomenon he called explanatory style. After every failure we tell ourselves a short story in our head about why things did not work out. The pessimistic version has three features: this situation will last forever, it will ruin everything for me, and it simply comes from the kind of person I am. The optimistic version says that the trouble will pass and concerns only this one matter, and that there were many causes, my mistake being only one of them.

These two ways of explaining failure have very real consequences. In the mid-1980s, the same researcher studied agents at a large American insurance company, people working in a job where they often met with refusal. The results were telling: agents with a more optimistic explanatory style sold over a third more policies, and they were also less likely to quit this demanding job.

Realistic optimism, however, does not mean ignoring risk. A pessimist with a fever immediately assumes pneumonia, while a naive optimist ignores the symptoms and heads for the airport regardless. A realistic optimist expects to get better but goes to the doctor anyway, and then checks whether the flight can be rescheduled. Callahan was exactly this kind of optimist.

Most important of all, though, is that explanatory style can be changed. A meta-analysis of 29 studies, published in 2017, showed that optimism can be learned, although the effect is moderate and strongest right after the training. The method itself resembles a fair trial, in which every accusation requires evidence. When you catch yourself thinking something like “I’ll never manage it,” you cross-examine that thought like a witness. You check whether “never” is really justified in this case, and look for other explanations along the way.

sections.heading: Beyond Our Own Abilities
paragraphs: Psychologists distinguish optimism from hope. Charles Richard Snyder, a researcher at the University of Kansas, described hope in the early 1990s as a way of thinking made up of three elements. The first is a goal, the second is the ability to find routes that lead to it, and the third is the conviction that I am able to follow those routes, in other words a sense of agency. An optimist, Snyder observes, expects a good outcome but does not always have a plan for getting there. When the road is closed, an optimist can easily get stuck, whereas a person of hope starts looking for a detour.

Snyder’s team tested how much this kind of hope matters in ordinary life. In a study published in 2002, 213 first-year students filled in a short hope questionnaire, and the researchers followed their progress at college for six years. The result was thought-provoking. Among those who scored high on the scale, nearly 57 percent graduated, compared with only 40 percent of those who scored low.

That is an apt description of everyday hope, which serves us well at school and at work. But it has the same limit as optimism. Each of its elements depends on us: on our goals, our routes and our strength. Both of them involve an assessment of our own abilities, and that assessment has to take the facts into account. Positive thinking helps in many things, but at the death of someone close, or in the face of a serious diagnosis, it is no longer enough.

Callahan understood this well. His calm came from doing what he could and looking honestly at what was beyond his control. Once a person has done everything in their power, explanatory style alone is no longer enough. Is there anything, then, that we can lean on, regardless of our own chances?

sections.heading: Abraham Counted the Years
paragraphs: In his Letter to the Romans, the apostle Paul describes a man for whom, humanly speaking, there was no hope left. Abraham was about a hundred years old, and his wife Sarah had long been unable to have children. Yet God promised him descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky (Genesis 15:5). Paul sums up his attitude in a paradox: “Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed” (Romans 4:18) that he would become the father of many nations.
Paul states clearly whom Abraham trusted: “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist” (Romans 4:17). The patriarch, then, placed his hope in a specific Person.

The most interesting part, though, is the next sentence: “Without weakening in his faith, he acknowledged the decrepitness of his body” (Romans 4:19). The Greek word rendered here as “acknowledged” means looking at something closely and weighing the matter carefully. Some older translations, the King James Version among them, rendered it the other way around, as though Abraham had paid no attention to his body. The oldest Greek manuscripts, however, give us the picture of a man who looked the facts straight in the face, counted his years, and did not pretend to be younger.

This is exactly where the line runs between optimism and biblical hope. Optimism looks for a favorable explanation in the facts, but Abraham found none and did not even try to invent one. His hope rested on something else entirely. Paul writes that he was “fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised” (Romans 4:21). What he leaned on, then, was the character of the One who had made the promise. The Letter to the Hebrews adds a picture that every new wave would have brought to Callahan’s mind. It calls hope an anchor, “firm and secure,” reaching behind the curtain, where Jesus entered first on our behalf (Hebrews 6:19-20). An anchor does not hold a boat because the sea happens to be calm. It holds because it has caught on a seabed that cannot be seen from the deck, and although the waves may run high, the boat stays where it is. In the earthly temple, the curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s presence, and the author of the letter says that Jesus, as our high priest, has appeared before the very face of God. The anchor of hope, then, is fastened to the One who is already on the other side.

sections.heading: What Does It All Rest On?
paragraphs: The New Testament is very specific about why this anchor holds. The apostle Peter writes of God: “By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). Christian hope, then, does not grow out of a sunny temperament or favorable calculations. It grows out of a specific event: the One who died on the cross came out of the tomb on the third day. Paul says openly that without Christ’s resurrection faith would be futile, and immediately adds that Christ has been raised as the first of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:17-20).

This hope is also bound up with waiting for a specific event. Paul describes the life of Christians as a time lived in a particular attitude: “as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). Jesus promised that He would return, and on the day of His coming those who died trusting Him will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16). That is why the apostle asks us, even at the graveside, not to grieve like people who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The God whom Abraham trusted showed, in the resurrection of Jesus, that He has the power to raise the dead.

What does all this mean for someone who has simply had a bad week? Both things are needed. An honest explanatory style is a skill worth practicing like any other, and Christians have no reason to give it up. They can calmly catch pessimistic thoughts, test them one by one, and look for new routes to their goals.

Biblical hope, on the other hand, is trust in Someone who keeps His word, and even a person with a gloomy temperament can have it. God does not promise that everything in your life will turn out the way you would like. He promises Himself, His faithfulness and the morning of the resurrection, and no forecast can measure that.

In everyday practice, these two things work together. You do what you can, and you don’t deceive yourself about the facts. And what is beyond your control you entrust to God, whose faithfulness does not depend on your chances. Hope understood this way also needs practice. You practice it every day by turning your thoughts back to the One who left the tomb on Easter morning and who promised that He would return.

Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: What do I rest my hope on when the facts are no longer on my side?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Recall one failure from the past few days and think about the story you tell yourself about it. Does the word “always” or “never” appear in that story? Consider on Whom, or on what, you want to rest your hope today.

**In action.** Today, tell one person close to you about that failure, briefly and without dressing it up. It could be a conversation over a cup of tea or a phone call on your way home. Ask them for one thing: to help you find a more honest explanation than “always,” for example by pointing out what was temporary and what this matter really does not touch. Finally, tell them what you rest your hope on when your own chances look slim. If you have no one to talk to today, write down on a piece of paper what a friend would say to you, and slip it into your Bible at the Letter to the Romans.
